item.content:encoded:
The Red Sox clinched a playoff spot on Sept. 20 by losing, 5-1, to the Rays in Tampa. Their ticket to October got punched about an hour later anyway, when the Braves beat the Astros three time zones away.
Nobody in that clubhouse watched themselves get in.
Rewind five months. Alex Cora got fired on a Saturday morning in April, with Boston sitting at 10-17. By June 24, the Red Sox were 15.5 games back in the AL East, with playoff odds cratered to 8.4%. That’s about as buried as a team gets in June.
Chad Tracy took over that wreckage on April 26 with zero big-league managing experience. Since then, Boston has gone 74-55 under him, a .573 winning percentage that would put most division leaders to shame. From July 27 through the end of the regular season, they played at a .609 clip, 28-18 down the stretch. They’re the first team in MLB history to lose 46 of their first 78 games and still finish above .500. Not one hot month. The roster Tracy built out of the wreckage. It’s the exact arc Central Maine tracked: a dreadful start, then a red-hot summer.
That’s the case for the permanent job. Not vibes. Receipts.
Beat writer Tyler Milliken called it one of the most improbable summers in baseball history, and he’s not exaggerating. A team that lost its manager in a firing nobody saw coming turned around and finished with the second-best road winning percentage in the American League.
This tweet nails how Saturday actually felt in that clubhouse:
Anticlimactic clinch, but to be on pace to go down as one of the worst Red Sox teams ever, then lock in, ignore the noise, and go on a generational run that led to postseason baseball…that’s both incredibly impressive and very much worth celebrating. See you in the Bronx. pic.twitter.com/ETJ7MEnHsj
— Jared Carrabis (@Jared_Carrabis) September 20, 2026
Anticlimactic, sure. You don’t draw up “clinch while getting shut down by Tampa’s bullpen” as the moment. But in a 162-game season, sometimes the celebration starts because of somebody else’s scoreboard, and you find out standing at your locker.
Plenty of the beat corps agrees on where the conversation goes next.
The Red Sox were 10-17 when Chad Tracy took over. A first time manager with no big league experience. He walked into a clubhouse of players that just lost a well-liked and respected manager.
Things weren’t fixed instantly, but they didn’t need to be. They got there in the end,… pic.twitter.com/etkqeb1PUe
— Gordo (@BOSSportsGordo) September 20, 2026
Gordo’s calling for a Manager of the Year case, and he’s not wrong to. Tracy walked into a room that had just lost a manager players actually liked, and he didn’t need some big culture-reset speech to fix it. He kept writing lineups, put Roman Anthony in the leadoff spot down the stretch, and let a talented roster figure itself out.
None of this happened by accident. firebrandal.com made the case for Tracy back in July, and it’s only gotten stronger since, even with the rotation health questions that never fully disappeared. Mickey Gasper’s hot stretch since his recall was part of the same story, a roster that kept finding useful players in June, July and August while the rest of the sport had already buried them.
Mike Mutnansky put it best: when the Red Sox fired Cora on a Saturday morning in April, nobody thought this team would sniff October. Now they’re one of 12 clubs still alive for a title. They’ll open as the No. 2 wild card, likely on the road against the Yankees, so nobody’s handing them anything in the Bronx.
Doesn’t matter how they get in. Tracy got them here. Give the guy the job.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox woke up on Sunday knowing they could punch their ticket to the postseason in one of two ways.
They could beat the Tampa Bay Rays in their series finale, or the Atlanta Braves could defeat the Houston Astros in theirs.
A first-inning shellacking put Boston’s fate in the Braves’ hands, as the Rays ultimately took the series with a 5-1 victory.
Left-hander Patrick Sandoval needed 40 pitches to complete the nine-batter frame. The first five Rays reached, and put up a 4-0 lead on back-to-back two-run base hits by centerfielder Jonny DeLuca (double) and left-fielder Chandler Simpson (single) before the Red Sox starter could record an out. Sandoval issued his second walk of the inning to Victor Mesa Jr. before he finished the frame and stranded two runners.
“Nightmare, like legit nightmare situation,” a grimacing Sandoval told reporters postgame of the first inning. “Couldn’t really where my arm was in space, grip on the ball wasn’t great. Just a literal nightmare.”
Then came a complete 180. Sandoval looked like a new man when he returned for the bottom of the second. He set the Rays down in order on eight pitches, then needed six to do so again in the third.
Sandoval retired eight consecutive Rays before Mesa homered with one out in the fourth to push the lead to five. But it marked Tampa Bay’s fourth and final hit of the day; Sandoval retired his last 11 batters, and newly-returned righty Tyron Guerrero extended the streak to 14 with a 1-2-3 eighth.
Yet the Red Sox, who left 17 men on base over the first two games of the series, were blanked by righty Griffin Jax and the Rays bullpen until a brief rally bid in the top of the ninth. Boston out-hit Tampa Bay 6-4, but went 0 for 4 with runners in scoring position, and stranded six.
Roman Anthony led off the game with a groundball single to right, but he was erased and replaced when catcher Adley Rutschman popped into a force out. The Red Sox did not put another man on base until Rutschman singled with one out in the fourth, an opportunity quickly erased by shortstop Trevor Story grounding into an inning-ending double play.
Boston’s best chance came and went in Jax’s fifth and final frame, when they loaded the bases on a one-out single by third baseman Caleb Durbin, and walks to centerfielder Jarren Duran and right-fielder Nate Eaton. Jax, who had not exceeded 67 pitches in a start since Aug. 2, was up to 69 when Anthony came to bat with two outs and the bases loaded. It took five pitches to end the threat; Anthony swung and missed at Jax’s last two, a 95.3 mph sinker and 90.2 mph changeup.
Much like Saturday’s 2-1 loss, Boston had no hope against the Tampa Bay bullpen. The Red Sox went in order against Cole Sulser in the sixth, and Brody Hopkins in the seventh.
Facing 2025 Red Sox trade deadline acquisition Steven Matz in the eighth, Anthony doubled with two outs. Jahmai Jones came in to pinch-hit for designated hitter Mickey Gasper. Jones has dominated left-handed pitching since the Red Sox acquired him from the Detroit Tigers during the All-Star break, but Matz struck him out swinging on four pitches.
After his 40-pitch first, Sandoval completed his remaining six innings on a mere 54. He became just the fourth Red Sox pitcher in the last 26 years, and first since Rick Porcello in 2016, to pitch at least seven innings after giving up at least four runs in the first. Sandoval yielded five earned runs on four hits, walked two (both in the first), and struck out five over seven innings. He threw 73.4% of his 94 pitches for strikes.
Activated from the injured list Sunday morning, Guerrero was sharp in his first inning of work since Aug. 31. The towering righty retired the Rays’ No. 2-4 batters, including American League home-run leader Junior Caminero, in order on 12 pitches (nine strikes). Guerrero’s return will bolster a Boston bullpen currently without closer Aroldis Chapman (day-to-day with lat tightness), and righty Justin Slaten (season-ending flexor injury).
Story ensured the Red Sox would not be shut out. His fifth home run of the year, off righty Ty Johnson, soared 405 feet to left at 102.7 mph with one out in the ninth.
Thus concludes the final Red Sox road trip of the season. They went 2-4 against the Texas Rangers and Rays, were outscored 23-15, and left 42 men on base.
After an off-day Monday, their final homestand of the season begins Tuesday night against the Cleveland Guardians.
But first, all eyes turn to the Braves and Astros.

item.content:encoded:
The Yankees’ odds of winning the AL East are down to 2.8 percent per FanGraphs after getting walked off by the Diamondbacks last night. I know mathematically that makes sense, but the chances mentally feel even more extreme. I’ve been having “fun” (or whatever) comping the odds to certain pitchers from history getting a hit. We are the dregs. Remember mid-2000s Mets pitcher Aaron Heilman? I personally remember him most for giving up the homer to Yadier Molina late in Game 7 of the 2006 NLCS, just before Adam Wainwright famously caught Carlos Beltrán looking to win the pennant.
Anyway, Heilman was a horrendous hitter. He singled once in his rookie year, and then never got another hit. He ended his career 1-for-47, so an .021 average. So the Yankees just need magic only a little bit more sufficient than that RBI single by Heilman off Sidney Ponson on August 12, 2003! Hell yeah.
It’s not happening, but we press on because it’s good to check up on what everyone else is doing anyway. Here’s what was going on Saturday.
Tampa Bay Rays (94-60) 2, Boston Red Sox (84-71) 1
The Yankees gained a full game on the Rays on Friday for the first time in over a week, as Boston snapped their six-game winning streak. There was no such fortune to be found yesterday though; Tampa Bay made sure of that well before first pitch in Arizona, and it only got worse from there. By the end of the night, the Rays once again had a five-game lead over the Yanks; Tampa Bay’s magic number (combination of Rays wins or Yankees losses) to clinch the AL East is four.
This one was a pitchers’ duel to the bitter end. Brayan Bello had easily his best outing of a turbulent season (and probably the best of his career), firing eight shutout frames at the Trop and fanning 11 Rays, tying a personal best from July 9, 2024. As he only went 5.1 in that one and faced merely the soon-to-depart-Oakland A’s rather than the division-leading Rays.
The only true blemish on Bello’s record came when Jonathan Aranda cracked an opposite-field homer to make it a 1-1 game in the fourth. Tampa Bay had a chance to make it 2-1 against Bello in the seventh when Liam Hicks and Chandler Simpson led off with singles. Bello then induced a grounder from Victor Mesa Jr. to move up the runners, and then another off the bat of Richie Palacios to Trevor Story, who nailed pinch-runner Jonny DeLuca at home. Palacios swiped second, but Bello fanned Cedric Mullins to end the inning. The Rays went down in order in the eighth to end Bello’s brilliant night.
Unfortunately for Bello, a win wasn’t in the cards because Boston put up next to nothing against Freddy Peralta and the Rays’ pitching staff. Doubles by Caleb Durbin and Roman Anthony gave the Red Sox their one run in the second, but they were stymied from there. They had chances!
- Second inning after Anthony’s two-out double: Mickey Gasper lineout to center
- Fourth inning with runners on first and second, one out: Story strikeout, Durbin popout
- Fifth inning with runner on second, one out: Anthony groundout, Gasper strikeout
- Sixth inning with runners on first and second, two out: Durbin fly out to left
- Eighth inning after Adley Rutschman’s one-out double: Wilyer Abreu strikeout, Nick Sogard lineout
Even against lockdown Rays closer Bryan Baker, Boston had one last shot to take a late lead. After Story grounded out, Durbin lined a double down the left field line to put himself in scoring position for Jarren Duran. Durbin darted from second, however, and got thrown out stealing third. Duran promptly followed with a triple over DeLuca’s head in center. Isiah Kiner-Falefa bounced one to Junior Caminero at third to end the threat.
Granted a chance to walk it off, Tampa Bay didn’t waste it. Rather than blasting a homer to finish the game as he had twice earlier this homestand, Caminero began the ninth against Garrett Whitlock with a single to left. (A catwalk curtailed Durbin’s effort to catch a popup earlier in the AB.) DeLuca popped up, but Chandler Simpson grounded one through the six-hole for another hit. The runners moved up when catcher Connor Wong let a Whitlock sinker up bounce off his glove for a passed ball. Palacios ended the night with flare to center that fell in, securing the win for Tampa Bay. At least the Wild Card Series is also almost certainly going to be at Yankee Stadium now, I suppose.
AL Rock Fight
Cleveland Guardians (80-75) 12, The Athletics (61-94) 6
Two crooked numbers effectively decided Saturday’s affair with the A’s in a hurry. Tanner Bibee kind of stunk and would allow six runs in a dozen hits while failing to make through five, but it hardly mattered. Cleveland erased a 2-0 deficit in the first on a three-run shot from rookie Chase DeLauter and two-run homer by Angel Martinez. The A’s got one back in the third, only to see another five-spot from the Guardians on poor Jacob Lopez as David Fry, Austin Hedges, and Brayan Rocchio all delivered RBI doubles. Martinez later added a homer and an RBI single in a career-best four-hit day.
Chicago White Sox (79-76) 3, Detroit Tigers (73-82) 1
Cleveland’s win meant that Chicago was stuck at a game back in the AL Central in the best-case, but they did at least help push one of their Wild Card foes out of the picture with a win. Honestly, this was probably kind of a dud of a game for anyone who isn’t a White Sox fan, the lone highlights being Sean Burke’s six scoreless frames and Miguel Vargas’ sixth-inning solo shot to make it 3-1, Chicago (the other runs scored on an RBI single by Munetaka Murakami and a fifth-inning sac fly). Spencer Torkelson had a chance to tie the game with a homer following Hao-Yu Lee’s two-out single in the ninth, but he flew out to center to end it.
Milwaukee Brewers (97-58) 1, Baltimore Orioles (75-80) 0
Yeah, it’s time to stick a fork in the O’s. It was all but certain for awhile now, but Chicago’s win combined with Baltimore’s second-straight loss to Milwaukee means that the Orioles are four back with a week to play, plus multiple teams in front of them. Trevor Rogers was the hard-luck loser here while Baltimore got blanked on four hits and Rece Hinds lost a fly ball from Joey Ortiz in the sun, allowing him to triple and score on Gary Sánchez’s RBI grounder. Woof.
Texas Rangers (78-77) 6, Toronto Blue Jays (76-79) 1
The O’s aren’t the only bird that are all but shot down, either. Trade Deadline acquisition José Soriano coughed up an early homer to Josh Jung, beginning a five-inning, six-run outing that pushed Toronto three games out in the Wild Card and the Rangers into a one-game AL West lead over Houston. The only downside for Texas was that second-half surprise Cal Quantrill—who has a 1.75 ERA since re-entering the rotation in late July—left in the second with lat tightness, so old friend Jordan Montgomery picked up the slack in long relief, retiring 11 of the 12 hitters he faced with no hits allowed.
Atlanta Braves (91-64) 6, Houston Astros (77-78) 3
Houston and Texas have been wrestling all week over the prestigious “Who can win this horri-awful division with a .500-ish record” crown. Sunday it went to Texas with the Astros falling out of their tie for first place (remember that they own the tiebreaker). Isaac Paredes had put Houston ahead with a solo homer and an RBI knock in the third, but the Astros’ bullpen set that lead on fire. The big blow came off the bat of Ronald Acuña Jr., who belted a grand slam off Bryan Abreu in the seventh after AJ Blubaugh made a right mess of things.

The Boston Red Sox and Tampa Bay Rays head into Sunday’s series finale at Fenway Park with the three-game set knotted at one win apiece after Saturday’s 2-1 Rays victory.
Left-hander Patrick Sandoval takes the mound for Boston against Tampa Bay right-hander Griffin Jax, a matchup that carries extra weight with the regular season winding down and playoff positioning still in flux.
Interim manager Chad Tracy has kept the bulk of his starting nine intact, but he has made a modest yet noticeable adjustment involving outfielder Jarren Duran, via Underdog MLB.
After sitting out the series opener and batting eighth on Saturday, Duran will slide up one spot into the seventh hole. He will hit in front of Isaiah Kiner-Falefa and Nate Eaton while remaining in center field, the position he has occupied since injuries to Ceddanne Rafaela and Eli White opened the job.
The rest of the order features Roman Anthony in left, Mickey Gasper at designated hitter, Adley Rutschman behind the plate, Trevor Story at shortstop, Nick Sogard at first, and Cooper Durbin at third.
The move comes during a difficult individual season for Duran. Entering Sunday he is hitting .206 in 144 games, with 65 runs, 110 hits, 20 home runs and 69 RBIs. His slugging percentage sits at .364 and his OPS at .626.
Speculation about a possible trade lingered for weeks before the August 4 deadline, yet Duran remained in a Red Sox uniform and has continued to receive regular playing time as the club pushes toward October.
Boston sits at 84-71 with seven games left and occupies what currently looks like the second American League Wild Card spot. Should the standings hold, the Red Sox would open the postseason on the road in a best-of-three Wild Card series against the New York Yankees.
Every remaining game, including Sunday’s finale against a familiar division rival, therefore carries playoff implications.
Tracy’s decision to bump Duran up in the order is a small tactical shift rather than a wholesale overhaul, but it signals a willingness to tinker as the club tries to generate more consistent offense down the stretch.
Whether the extra spot in the lineup produces results remains to be seen.
Duran’s season-long struggles have been well documented, yet he has shown flashes of the power and speed that once made him a fixture in the middle of Boston’s order.
A productive afternoon against Jax and the Rays would give the Red Sox a series victory and a bit of momentum heading into the final week.
With the calendar now late September and the postseason picture still taking shape, even incremental lineup changes can feel significant.

item.content:encoded:
Can you believe the playoffs are almost here? A week from today the Red Sox will wrap up their regular season, closing the book on what has been among the most unexpected, topsy turvy seasons we’ve ever seen. From there the playoffs await, and who knows what twists and turns may still be in store.
But before we get there, what business is there left for the Red Sox to get squared away before Game 1 of the Wild Card series? We answer your questions in today’s Red Sox mailbag.
Tanner Houck and Garrett Crochet both appear close to ready to return. What is the chance that the Red Sox decide to put both of them on the postseason roster? Each feels like a high upside question mark but is it too risky relying on both of them to excel in limited roles? — Paul from Bluesky
If the Red Sox decide they’re ready I think there’s a great chance both pitch in the playoffs. The question of whether or not it’s too risky is valid, but the other factor to consider is would it be riskier to let an inferior arm take the mound at Yankee Stadium with the season on the line.
The nature of a best-of-three playoff series compared to a best-of-five or even a best-of-seven also makes the idea of loading up on short-inning relievers more attractive.
The Red Sox will only need three starting pitchers in the first round, presumably Sonny Gray, Ranger Suarez and Payton Tolle, in some order. That effectively frees up two additional bullpen spots, one of which I’m guessing will be filled by Jake Bennett as an emergency bulk man should the starter exit early due to injury or poor performance.
The back end of the bullpen is pretty much set in stone. If everyone is healthy and available it will be Aroldis Chapman, Garrett Whitlock, Erik Miller and Tyron Guerrero locking down the high leverage innings. But after that the Red Sox have some interesting decisions to make.
In one group you have the other short men, including Greg Weissert, Jovani Moran and Wyatt Olds. Then in the next group you have the longer men, including Patrick Sandoval, Brayan Bello, Alec Gamboa and Raymond Burgos. Finally, you have Crochet, Houck and Johan Oviedo, who has also begun a rehab assignment after missing nearly the entire season. What the Red Sox have to decide is which five of those 10 options give you the best chance to win?
I don’t think you can dispute that Crochet and Houck have the highest ceiling of that bunch, so if they’re good to go I don’t think the Red Sox will hesitate to give them the nod.
With Romy Gonzalez now hitting so well in Worcester, do you see him being put on the postseason roster as a lefty masher, and one of Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Andruw Monasterio or Jahmai Jones being left off? — @wcbosox on Bluesky
If the Red Sox believe Romy Gonzalez gives them the best chance to win in October, I feel like it would make sense for them to call him up and get him some looks at big league pitching over the last two weeks. You could make a great case that they should — he was batting .360 in 23 games since being optioned to Triple-A entering Friday — but if that doesn’t happen then that could be a sign the Red Sox don’t see him as part of the October plan.
Either way, the club has some tough decisions to make as far as constructing the bench goes.
Presuming that Ceddanne Rafaela returns from the IL without any issues and Willson Contreras isn’t sidelined by his hand injury, the Red Sox should enter the playoffs with a starting lineup featuring Adley Rutschman at catcher, Contreras, Nick Sogard, Trevor Story and Caleb Durbin across the infield, and an outfield of Rafaela, Wilyer Abreu, Roman Anthony and Jarren Duran, with one of Anthony or Duran presumably starting at designated hitter if a righty is on the mound.
That leaves four spots for Kiner-Falefa, Monasterio, Jones, Mickey Gasper, Connor Wong, Nate Eaton, Gonzalez and possibly Curtis Mead. For our purposes we can probably set aside Eaton, who will likely be optioned upon Rafaela’s activation, as well as Mead, who only just started swinging a light bat and won’t have the benefit of a rehab assignment prior to his return.
Let’s also set aside some of the more outside the box candidates like Braiden Ward, who has never appeared in a big league game but who may garner consideration as a late-inning pinch runner after stealing 60 bases at Triple-A.
One spot will go to a backup catcher, and while you could talk yourself into Gasper filling that role, Wong has the most familiarity with the pitching staff and the Red Sox would probably rather keep Gasper available as a pinch hitter without worrying about catching logistics.
How about the other three spots? Kiner-Falefa, Monasterio and Gonzalez are all versatile infield defenders who bat right-handed, so there’s some redundancy there. Jones also bats right-handed and could function as an emergency reserve outfielder in addition to his pinch hitter, and while Gasper is technically a switch hitter, his real value comes from the left side, where he’s crushed righties over the past month.
What’s going to happen? My guess is the bench will be Wong, Gasper, Jones and one of the three righty infielders. So to go back to your original question, could Gonzalez make the playoff roster over one of Kiner-Falefa, Monasterio or Jones? Yes, and in fact even if he doesn’t make the roster one of those guys could still wind up on the outside looking in.
If the playoffs started today who would be the starting second baseman? Also, what’s the long-term plan for that position? — Tom P.
If the playoffs started today I think Nick Sogard would be the clear choice to start at second base. He’s been an everyday player for the Red Sox since the end of July, and at a time where most of the offense has hit a skid Sogard has been a reliable contributor at the plate, batting .262 with five home runs and a .772 OPS entering the weekend since being called back up on July 29.
Long-term, the Red Sox have a couple of different candidates who could emerge in the coming years.
If he hadn’t broken his wrist in his team debut I think it’s safe to say Curtis Mead would have spent the past two months starting at second for the Red Sox. Prior to the trade he was in the midst of a breakout season with the Washington Nationals, and at only 25 years old there’s good reason to believe his best years are still ahead of him. Whether he returns in the playoffs or for the start of next season, Mead should have the best chance to claim second base for himself.
But outside of him, Sogard and perhaps Gonzalez or Anthony Seigler, there is one other wild card. That’s Franklin Arias.
The top Red Sox prospect is putting the finishing touches on a brilliant season, and if he continues to develop he should have a great chance of becoming a key building block, perhaps as soon as next year. With Story under contract for only one more season he will have an opportunity to slide right into the starting shortstop job entering 2028, but what if he proves he’s ready for primetime before that? In that case Arias might get an initial look at second, with Mead perhaps rotating between the designated hitter spot and occasionally giving Durbin and Contreras a breather at their corner infield positions.
Does MLB need to readjust its postseason schedule? The No. 2 or 3 team in the American League will be eliminated in a three-game series, meanwhile two teams that are barely .500 play each other in the first round. — Brandon C.
I like the idea that there should be a reward for winning your division. If you’re one of the top two division winners you get a first round bye, and if you’re the third division winner you at least get to host the best-of-three Wild Card series. I’m fine with that, even in a weird year like this where all of the American League’s best teams are in the same division and the other division leaders are mediocre at best.
But the problem is what happens afterwards. Like you said, the No. 2 and 3 teams in the AL are probably going to wind up being the Yankees and Red Sox, and whichever of those teams advances will have to play the No. 1 seeded Tampa Bay Rays. Meanwhile, all three teams on the other side of the bracket could potentially finish with worse records than anyone on the AL East side, and one of those clubs will be guaranteed a trip to the ALCS.
I think MLB could address this by reseeding after the Wild Card round. The top two division winners would still get home field advantage in their divisional series, but whichever team advancing out of the Wild Card round has the better record would be paired with the second division winner. So this year if the Red Sox beat the Yankees and let’s say the AL West champion wins their Wild Card series, the Red Sox would go on to play the AL Central champion instead of the Rays, while the AL West champion would get Tampa Bay even though they would have technically started the playoffs as the higher seed.
Most years it probably won’t make a huge difference, but reseeding ahead of the divisional round would strike a balance between preserving the incentives for winning your division while ensuring the bracket doesn’t become unbalanced.

For 13 games in 2024, Mickey Gasper came up to the plate for the Boston Red Sox. In many cases, the NESN cameras cut to his eager parents as they awaited his first MLB hit.
A hit that never came. In 2024, at least.
Gasper’s journey to the big leagues was unconventional. He played at Bryant University, an NEC school whose only athletic national championship victory came from its athletic band and cheer team.
At the time, Bryant was a baseball team at the top of its conference. Gasper became a major part of this sustained success, as he dominated in his sophomore, junior, and senior seasons, both with Bryant and in summer leagues. This included the Cape Cod Baseball League, the most competitive summer baseball circuit in the country.
But this success never fully translated to his first few seasons in pro ball.
Gasper was drafted by the Yankees in the 27th round of the 2018 MLB Draft. This round doesn’t even exist in 2026. Without the pedigree of a top-round talent, Gasper did not receive the benefit of the doubt for his skills in the minor leagues. Instead, he bounced around, climbed slowly, and eventually, after a 2024 hot streak, got the call-up to Boston at 28 years old.
2024: no hits in Boston. 2025: a .488 OPS in Minnesota. It looked as if the sun may have finally set on Gasper’s chance to be a big league mainstay.
Then came one of the crazier “Linsanity”-adjacent runs Red Sox fans have seen. But with the hot streak still burning fingers, the baseball world is pondering… is this a two-month heater or a sign of things to come?
Let’s dive into the numbers behind Gasper’s career-defining stretch at age 30.
Stats updated prior to games on September 17.
What Do the Underlying Numbers Say?
Gasper’s underlying numbers say two very different things. On one hand, his .373 OBP is backed up by a patient approach and strong understanding of the strike zone. His power, however, is reflected highly in his expected stats, while his bat speed and exit velocities show signs of regression.
In many ways, Gasper’s lack of elite athleticism or power on the surface makes his hot streak all the more impressive. He doesn’t have quick enough hands to generate major power or hit to all fields at an elite level. Instead, he chooses his battles remarkably well.
This mix of extreme patience, including a 15.0% strikeout rate and 12.6% walk rate, allows Gasper to maintain an All-Star-caliber xSLG and xwOBA. His exit velocity and hard-hit rate are average at best, but because he is so patient, Gasper picks his spots well. This means that he’s one of the league’s best in squared-up percentage.
This squared-up percentage could be a number that regresses over time, but Gasper’s breakout is supported in part by the underlying numbers. You can teach plate discipline, but it’s very hard to do this without compromising a hitter’s typical approach at the plate. Thankfully for Gasper, his plate discipline is a skill that gives him a higher floor at the MLB level.
In essence, Gasper is a player with a high floor and occasional bursts of a high ceiling. In many ways, he derives his value in similar ways to streaky, defense-first center fielders. He should generate value with the skills he is good at and occasionally go on hot streaks strong enough to carry a team on his back for a short period of time.
The one problem with this high ceiling is that Gasper is a positionless player. He played much of his career as a catcher, and Boston still has Gasper catch the occasional game. He has also played second base and left field in his MLB career, but these are not positions where fans can feel overly comfortable with him defensively.
If Gasper excels defensively at first or second base, there is certainly a chance he could become a mainstay. However, if he continues to produce fielding run values in the negatives, then he could lose opportunities to earn contracts or stay on MLB rosters as a reserve.
Comparing “Linsanity”-adjacent MLB Streaks
Basketball fans remember the magical season of Jeremy Lin, the Harvard graduate who got his shot with the Knicks due to injury and went on an all-time short-term run. Shortly after, he disappeared from the NBA world with an incredible legacy.
Gasper could go a few different directions in his career. Either he becomes a mainstay in the center of a lineup, a role player for years to come, or a minor league bat who bounces around other leagues as he ages.
Here are two similar runs where a player’s MLB tenure was dominant, but not long-lasting.
Yermin Mercedes
When the average American hears the word “Mercedes,” they probably think of the luxury car brand. When baseball diehards hear the word, they think of Yermin.
After April of 2024, the White Sox designated hitter/catcher was hitting over .400 with an OPS over 1.000 and five home runs. By June, Mercedes’ performance had slipped so mightily that he was sent back to the minor leagues.
After an underwhelming comeback attempt with San Francisco in 2022, Mercedes jumped around to select minor league teams. He last played in the Dominican and Mexican Winter Leagues in their 2024-25 seasons. He produced an OPS below .600 with both teams.
Aristides Aquino
It’s long been said that the best hitters are the ones who punish pitchers the most for each mistake they make on the mound. So when a 25-year-old, 6-foot-4, 220-pound outfielder out of the Dominican Republic was nicknamed “The Punisher,” he turned a lot of heads.
This is Aristides Aquino. At the time, there was a genuine belief that Aquino would turn the Cincinnati Reds around after a rough few seasons. They became the quintessential “underrated” pick entering 2020, so much so that they were not underrated at all.
And while the Reds did make the postseason in 2020, this was thanks to the expanded playoffs more than Aquino.
In 2019, Aquino hit for an .891 OPS across 56 games. The major difference, however, between Aquino and Gasper lies in the underlying metrics. Aquino struggled with plate discipline, whiffed at a high rate, and held expected stats that were far lower than his actual metrics. His slugging percentage, for example, was .576 in 2019 compared to an xSLG of .503.
His numbers in 2020 dipped and never quite recovered. In Aquino’s final season in 2022, he struggled at the plate again, but still produced a 1.3 rWAR thanks in large part to his impressive speed and 99th percentile arm strength.
Is Age Truly Just a Number?
Gasper is 30 years old. If the Red Sox make the ALCS, then Gasper will turn 31 at the start of that series. Mercedes was 28 during his “Linsanity” run, while Aquino was 25.
Obviously, this late start will eliminate certain achievements that Gasper can no longer pursue. But this isn’t just a lucky start for Gasper. He’s filled with highly sustainable underlying metrics that show his potential as an on-base threat for years to come.

item.content:encoded:
This has been a rough stretch for the Red Sox offense, which has effectively turned into a pumpkin after a torrid two months this summer. This week in particular the bats have fallen silent, and for much of Thursday night the Red Sox looked like they were headed toward a discouraging series sweep at the worst possible time.
Things took an especially grim turn when Willson Contreras left the game in the eighth inning after being hit in the hand by a pitch, but while the specter of his absence will loom over the club in the days to come, Trevor Story once again proved that you can never count this Red Sox team out.
The veteran shortstop came through with a go-ahead three-run home run in the top of the eighth inning, flipping the script and giving the Red Sox a badly needed 4-3 win to avoid a sweep at the hands of the Texas Rangers.
Story’s shot came with one out against Rangers closer Jacob Latz, completing a three-run comeback and cutting Boston’s magic number to clinch a playoff spot to three with nine games remaining.
“To steal that last one is huge,” Story told NESN’s Jahmai Webster postgame. “It’s momentum we can ride out into Tampa.”
Prior to Story’s home run, Thursday was shaping up to be among the club’s worst losses of the season.
A hallmark of the offense’s struggles early in the year was a lot of empty, uncompetitive at-bats, tons of swing and miss and a general inability to make good contact. Even with the Rangers opting for a bullpen game led by Cody Bradford, whose fastball averages just 88.6 mph, the Red Sox couldn’t square anything up.
The Red Sox only managed two hits through the first five innings, both singles in the fourth inning. That put runners at the corners with two outs, but Jarren Duran grounded out to squander the opportunity.
It was a similar story in the sixth, when Wilyer Abreu singled and Adley Rutschman finally did some damage with a ground-rule double into the left-field gap. Had the ball stayed in play, Abreu probably would have scored, but instead the Red Sox had two men in scoring position for Story, who worked a full count and struck out to end the threat.
The offense did nothing to pick up Sonny Gray, who wasn’t perfect but did everything he could to keep the Red Sox in the game.
The veteran right-hander allowed a solo home run to Josh Jung with two outs in the first, and in the second he walked the first two batters of the inning, both of whom came around to score on an RBI bloop single by Danny Jansen and a run-scoring squeeze bunt by Evan Carter.
Gray settled down afterward and retired 14 of the last 16 batters he faced from the second inning into the seventh. He was charged with three runs over 6 1/3 innings and limited the Rangers to three hits and three walks with six strikeouts.
“I thought he was awesome,” Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy said. “The only blemish was the two walks, we kind of walked ourselves into the part of their lineup where they can play baseball a little bit with bunts and they drop a flare into center and there’s a safety squeeze, outside of that, that was a really, really good effort.”
Even when the Red Sox finally scored in the top of the seventh, they did so without recording a hit. Nate Eaton and Caleb Durbin led off with consecutive walks and Eaton advanced to third after Nick Sogard hit a rocket of a fly out to the center field wall. But with one out and a chance to fight back into the game, Roman Anthony grounded into a run-scoring fielder’s choice to make it 3-1. He advanced to second after the Rangers threw away the double-play attempt, but Mickey Gasper grounded out to end the inning.
Then came the eighth.
Once again the Red Sox got two men on base right away, with Abreu drawing a leadoff walk before Contreras was hit in the right hand by a pitch. He immediately left the game with the trainer and was replaced at first by Isiah Kiner-Falefa, but while the Red Sox worried about their slugger, the Rangers pulled Jakob Junis for their closer Latz, who has been among the most dominant closers in the American League this year.
Latz drew a pop out from Rutschman, but then Story stepped up to the plate and everything changed.
“You see one of our guys keeled over holding his hand and you’re down in the dumps seeing that and moments later the whole dugout erupts,” Tracy said. “We haven’t been doing much offensively for a few days and to get a swing right there and feel like you steal a game, it was enormous. Big emotion swing.”
With the lead in hand, Wyatt Olds and Alec Gamboa pitched a scoreless eighth, and with Aroldis Chapman unavailable, Garrett Whitlock came on for the ninth and locked down the save for the win. Story and Sogard turned inning-ending double plays in both the eighth and the ninth to ensure the Rangers couldn’t mount one last comeback.
“Good teams find a way to win and we’ve been doing that in the second half and that’s kind of who you become,” Story said. “And you feel that momentum, you feel that vibe around the game and we never give up.”
X-rays negative, Chapman day-to-day
The Red Sox got some good news postgame when X-rays on Contreras’ hand came back negative.
“He’s got a bruise on the hand and some swelling,” Tracy said. “So we’ll just take it day to day and see how he is.”
Tracy also confirmed that Chapman has been dealing with some lat tightness for the past few days and they are taking a conservative approach.
“It’s getting better but have to make sure it gets there, that’s why he wasn’t available tonight,” Tracy said, adding that an IL stint isn’t being considered for Chapman right now.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox are still sitting comfortably in the second Wild Card spot, but there are several issues they must resolve before they start thinking about playoff baseball.
Boston is a mediocre 11-11 over its last 22 games. While that's been good enough to sustain its playoff position, its play hasn't exactly inspired optimism for a deep postseason run.
Most of the Red Sox' problems can be linked to their underperforming lineup. Key hitters like Roman Anthony, Willson Contreras, Adley Rutschman and Wilyer Abreu have been concerningly inconsistent.
A deeper dive into the numbers suggests the struggling Sox will have their work cut out for them in their presumed Wild Card Series rematch at Yankee Stadium. Here are the club's five biggest areas of concern with 10 games remaining:
Roman Anthony is ice-cold
The Red Sox need Roman Anthony to be one of their best offensive players to have any chance of a deep postseason run. If the former No. 1 prospect continues to play the way he has for most of September, that will be problematic.
Anthony is hitting just .149 (7-for-47) with one home run and a .428 OPS over his last 11 games. He has struck out 18 times in 51 plate appearances.
The 22-year-old's struggles beg the question: should he still be the leadoff hitter in the postseason? Interim manager Chad Tracy will have no choice but to reevaluate Anthony's spot in the lineup if his woes continue. The problem with that is there aren't any exciting alternatives. The leadoff spot has been a glaring issue all season long, regardless of who has been thrust into the role.
Struggling against high velocity
The Red Sox offense has been inconsistent no matter who's on the mound, but it has mostly struggled against pitchers with high velo. Here's how some of Boston's regulars have fared this season against pitches greater than or equal to 97 mph:
- Wilyer Abreu: .170 BA, .623 OPS (237 pitches)
- Jarren Duran: .065 BA, .300 OPS (203 pitches)
- Willson Contreras: .170 BA, .512 OPS (166 pitches)
- Ceddanne Rafaela: .205 BA, .449 OPS (157 pitches)
- Roman Anthony: .091 BA, .440 OPS (58 pitches)
- Adley Rutschman: .077 BA, .451 OPS (57 pitches)
The Red Sox' top performer against high velocity (97 mph and above) has been Caleb Durbin (.364 BA, .912 OPS, 161 pitches).
Being so vulnerable against high velocity will especially be a problem for Boston in its expected Wild Card Series matchup against the New York Yankees. Cy Young frontrunner and likely Game 1 starter Cam Schlittler averages 98 mph with his four-seam fastball, which he uses 44.5 percent of the time. Gerrit Cole averages 96.9 mph with his four-seam, using it 49.3 percent of the time.
Leaving runners stranded
Boston has been below average all season at capitalizing on runners in scoring position. It currently ranks 17th in batting average (.250) and 21st in OPS (.731) with RISP. They're hitting just .212 in such situations through 14 games so far in September.
The Yankees' elite pitching staff probably won't provide the Red Sox with many scoring opportunities in their short series, so it's imperative that they come through when given the chance. Lately, Boston hasn't had anyone in its lineup to feel confident about when they step to the plate with runners on.
Role players regressing
As great as guys like Willson Contreras, Caleb Durbin, and Wilyer Abreu were throughout the Red Sox' incredible midseason turnaround, it was the role players who powered their surge. Mickey Gasper, Jahmai Jones, Nick Sogard, Anthony Seigler, and Andruw Monasterio were instrumental in resurrecting Boston's season.
Gasper has cooled off, though no one expected him to sustain his Barry Bonds-like run. Jahmai Jones is 4 for his last 22 (.182) with nine strikeouts, suddenly making him a playoff roster cut candidate. Sogard is still hitting, but his .758 OPS so far in September suggests regression to the mean. Seigler is hurt. Monasterio posted a .578 OPS in August and is 0-for-11 so far in September, putting him on the playoff roster bubble.
That group deserves immense credit for getting the Red Sox here, but it cannot be counted on to propel the club through the postseason.
Erik Miller experiencing command issues
Boston's bullpen is arguably its biggest strength heading into the postseason. The back end with Garrett Whitlock, Tyron Guerrero, and Aroldis Chapman is elite.
We would've included trade deadline addition Erik Miller in that group last month, when he allowed only one earned run with 20 strikeouts and just three walks across his first 11 appearances with the Red Sox. His performance so far this month, however, has been alarming.
Miller, acquired from the San Francisco Giants in the Marcelo Mayer trade, has allowed four earned runs with six walks and six strikeouts through five appearances (4.1 IP) in September. His command struggles were a question mark upon his joining the club, and it appears that issue has reemerged with less than two weeks until the playoffs.
After Wednesday's poor outing against the Texas Rangers (2 H, 3 ER, 1 BB), Miller attributed his recent struggles to his mechanics. The Red Sox will hope that whatever the problem is, it's a quick fix, because Miller will be counted on to be their most reliable left-handed reliever not named Aroldis Chapman.

item.content:encoded:
If there has been one player on the 2026 Boston Red Sox who has had a polarizing season, it would be speedy outfielder Jarren Duran.
This past offseason, Duran was talked about as a potential trade chip, but Boston didn't make a move. The same can be said about the 2026 trade deadline as well. Boston has stuck by Duran, despite the fact that he is in the middle of the most difficult season of his career to this point. Duran has played in 142 games for Boston this season and he is slashing .204/.260/.360 with a .621 OPS, 20 home runs, 69 RBIs, 19 stolen bases, 15 doubles, four triples and 65 runs scored.
Despite the fact that Duran has had a tough season, Boston has arguably made the right call by sticking with him. There are positives when it comes to Duran. Right now, he's in the 92nd percentile in baserunning run value and the 90th percentile in outs above average. It's been tough for Duran to consistently get on base, but when he has gotten on base, he's a problem for opposing clubs. Also, he's been very good defensively this season. Roman Anthony missed months of action due to injury and Duran has stepped up with potentially the best defensive season of his career. In comparison, last year Duran was in the 18th percentile in outs above average. He has shown clear growth defensively and that shouldn't be ignored.
Boston Made The Right Call
Shockingly, Duran is one homer away from tying his career high of 21. Duran is also fourth on the Red Sox in RBIs with 69. If he can steal one more base this season, he'll record just his second 20-20 season of his big league career to this point.
There's no denying the fact that Duran has had a tough season overall. Right now, his OPS+ is 74. In comparison, it was 114 last year. He has regressed offensively and has struggled to get on base. But his defense has been really good, he has been a menace on the basepaths and he has been better than most on the club when runners have been on base. With his overall struggles, his trade value was very low this summer. If Boston has dealt him, imagine where the club would be right now with both Ceddanne Rafaela and Eli White both hurt?
Duran has gotten consistent opportunities all season, in large part due to the injuries. When the playoffs come, if the Red Sox's outfield is at full strength, they could easily utilize an outfield of Anthony, Rafaela and Wilyer Abreu and someone else as the club's designated hitter, like Mickey Gasper. Even if Duran isn't a consistent piece in the playoff lineup, Boston could use his elite speed as a pinch runner.
Duran's season hasn't been up to his standards, but he has still helped the 2026 Red Sox overall and there's still time for more. If the Red Sox had flipped him for some sort of minor league project because his value was low, that likely wouldn't have helped the club down the stretch. Duran still can and then in the offseason Boston can figure out next steps.

item.content:encoded:
Red Sox Video
Roman Anthony couldn't put a ring on it. For more than two months, what had to have been one of the most annoying and nagging injuries kept Anthony out of the Boston Red Sox lineup. He had partially torn a ligament in his right ring finger. It wasn't some massive, noticeable, life-changing injury. It was just an ailment that made it really hard to swing a bat.
The Red Sox handled business in the meantime. They went on that franchise record-tying 15-game winning streak. They watched Ceddanne Rafaela become an All-Star. They saw Mickey Gasper temporarily turn into Ted Williams.
Then, in late August, Anthony came back. He was supposed to be the final piece to the puzzle. If the Red Sox were a good baseball team without Anthony, they could potentially be a great one with him -- at least, that's how the thinking went. The problem, though, is clear: Since Anthony has been back, he hasn't been quite right. He hasn't looked like a rising star. He's looked like a hitter who is recognizing that hitting is actually really, really hard.
There's not a whole lot of time for Anthony to right the ship before the postseason, but there's just enough time for Boston fans to hold out hope that he has (or will find) a solution.
If he's going to make fixes, it'll have to be in his approach at the plate, where he's whiffed at a 35% rate in September, including a stretch of 17 strikeouts in 35 plate appearances. Something clearly isn't quite right here, although it may not be as bad as you think.
Roman Anthony's Swing Looks Different When It Matters
One quick way to figure out what might be happening with a hitter who is striking out a lot is to fast forward directly to two-strike counts and see what's happening.
First, though, take a look at what Anthony looks like on the first pitch of an at-bat with two runners on base. This clip shows a wide stance that's slightly open, a strong leg kick, and Anthony's signature ability to stay through the baseball and drive it the other way:

Roman Anthony Since Returning From IL

AB: 61
R: 8
H: 16
HR: 3
RBI: 5
BB: 5
SO: 20
AVG: .262
OPS: .793 pic.twitter.com/zCDEPxL2xi

That's not the swing that Anthony has had lately on two strikes. If you want to be a sad Red Sox fan for a few minutes, this next video is for you (it shows Anthony's recent strikeout stretch). And if you watch closely, you'll see that not only is Anthony not setting up the same each time as on the hit in the video above. He's not even set up the same in all of these clips. Clearly, he's searching for a two-strike solution, but it's changing the openness of his stance, the height at which he stands, the level of his leg kick and even the apparent length of his swing:

Roman Anthony has struck out in 17 of his last 35 plate appearances, and his 2-strike approach has looked completely discombobulated. pic.twitter.com/r3q3tc5A64
— Stats (@redsoxstats) September 12, 2026
Some hitters change their approach with two strikes -- contact hitters in particular often get lower and choke up on the bat to have the best chance of putting the ball in play. But the big and strong Anthony, if he's going to do that, better at least stick to a plan. And it seems like right now he doesn't have one.
So we can see the video, and we can see the basic stats, but to further figure out what's been going wrong with Anthony, we decided to take a look at the metrics behind his swing itself.
Clearly, coming back from a finger injury and a long layoff could make hitting harder, but this isn't just about Anthony's .226 average and .677 OPS in September. The Red Sox need to figure out what's going on so they can address it and improve those numbers the rest of the way.
Lucky for us, Statcast has just about every metric you could possibly imagine, so it's possible to compare all sorts of things about Anthony's swing inputs and batted ball outputs from each month of his rookie season through right now.
Take, for example, his attack angle. That's the vertical direction the sweet spot is traveling when it hits the baseball. This month, Anthony has an attack angle of 16 degrees. When he had a .946 OPS in July of last year, it was 14 degrees. The only time it has ever been this high before was last September in a super small sample size (26 pitches seen). And while it may seem like a minor difference, it can prevent the ideal line drive from coming off Anthony's bat.
That's just one metric. The rest of his bat statistics actually seem fine. Nothing is weird about his bat speed or his swing length or his attack direction. There's nothing underlying there to be totally concerned about.
This is the part, Red Sox fans, where the news gets good.
Roman Anthony Is Actually Just Fine
Anthony's swing, while maybe a little tilted from its optimal self, doesn't seem broken. He's just whiffing a bit more than you'd want. It's also worth considering what happens when Anthony doesn't whiff.
When he's made contact the ball in September, Anthony has hit it harder than ever before. His previous best average exit velocity in a month was in July 2025, at 96.9 miles per hour.
Entering this week, Anthony has averaged 97.0 miles per hour of exit velocity on his batted balls in this month. He's had a hard-hit percentage of 63.6%, right about his career average, and he has the third-best single-month barrel rate of his career. The Red Sox obviously can't afford for him to keep whiffing on more than a third of the swings he takes, but we can also recognize that Anthony is oh so close to putting it back together again.

ARLINGTON -- Despite getting an early two-run homer from Willson Contreras and taking advantage of a handful of Rangers miscues, the Red Sox couldn’t hold off Texas in a 7-3 loss on Wednesday at Globe Life Field.
The loss, however, didn’t change Boston's position in the postseason race, as the club remained in the second AL Wild Card spot and maintained its five-game cushion over the White Sox after Chicago lost to the Guardians earlier Wednesday.
Roman Anthony opened the game with a four-pitch walk. After Jahmai Jones flied out, Wilyer Abreu grounded into a forceout but beat the relay throw to first to avoid the double play and keep the inning alive for Contreras.
“Those are important details,” Contreras said in Spanish. “They don’t go unnoticed because they matter a lot in this game.”
With the postseason nearing, those -- along with having success with ABS challenges -- are the types of details Contreras was glad to see the Red Sox execute, especially with close games likely to become more common down the stretch. Boston had six successful challenges Wednesday night, and catcher Adley Rutschman improved to 19-for-27 on ABS challenges since joining the Red Sox.
Contreras entered the night batting .563 in his career against Rangers starter MacKenzie Gore, and helped set up his two-run homer with an early ABS challenge on a called strike that missed the bottom of the zone. After the call was overturned, Contreras took advantage when Gore left an 87 mph slider over the middle of the plate, sending it out to left-center field for his 27th homer of the season and an early 2-0 Red Sox lead.
“Honestly, I really liked that challenge, because I was sure it was a little bit under,” Contreras said. “And after that, I had the opportunity to get a pitch a little bit higher and connect for a home run.”
Contreras’ familiarity with Gore has also helped. The two faced each other frequently when Gore was with the Nationals and Contreras played for the Cubs and Cardinals.
“I know him well and I know that he always makes one or two errors in a game, so I am always trying to be ready for that error, like today,” Contreras said. “I wasn’t looking for that pitch, I was just looking for him to miss his spot in the middle.”
It was Contreras’ 27th homer of the season and his first since Aug. 21 against the Giants.
Texas eventually erased that advantage, pulling even at 2 in the fourth, but the Rangers helped Boston regain the lead an inning later.
Caleb Durbin drew Boston’s third walk of the night against Gore to begin the fifth. Trevor Story then sent a liner toward third baseman Josh Jung, who was unable to make a play. Durbin immediately recognized the opportunity, rounding second and advancing to third as Jung was slow to get the ball back into the infield.
The sequence ended Gore’s night and brought right-hander Jakob Junis out of the Rangers' bullpen. As Junis came set to face pinch-hitter Mickey Gasper, the ball slipped out of his glove for a balk, allowing Durbin to score and put the Red Sox back in front.
“We're going through it a little bit,” interim manager Chad Tracy said. “We didn't create a ton of opportunities. Obviously, Willson with a big swing to give us the lead, and only a couple other chances. ... That's it. So really, [getting] three runs on the board with only three hits was good in that sense. But just not creating a ton of opportunities for ourselves today.”
The 3-2 lead was short-lived, as Texas answered in the bottom half of the fifth to tie the game again.
Boston’s starter, Jake Bennett, worked through a 26-pitch first inning, limiting Texas to one run despite allowing two doubles and a single, before giving up another run in the fourth.
The game turned in the seventh, when reliever Erik Miller allowed three runs on two hits. Texas added another run in the eighth off Raymond Burgos.
“As a team, I think we're doing the best we can to capitalize on every chance we have,” Contreras said. “We battle. We come here with the right mindset. We work hard. We work on details that we need to get better on.
“And sometimes it doesn't matter how hard you work. Sometimes the results are not gonna come. But you have to build off that. You have to take those types of games personal and get better for tomorrow.”

Since returning from injury on August 30, Roman Anthony has looked more like the 2025 version of himself than he did at the beginning of the season. He's hitting .258 with a .764 OPS. In his 15 games, he's got five RBI and six extra-base hits; it's good for a 109 WRC+. It's exactly what the Red Sox needed from him in his return from his May 4 injury.
The one thing Anthony has struggled with has been leading off the game. He has hit leadoff in every game he's played since his return and has only two singles, a double, and five strikeouts with no walks in that spot. It's probably time to have someone else lead off.
In his absence (May 5-August 29), Red Sox leadoff hitters had success in the first inning. While they only hit .213, they had a .307 on-base percentage and a .449 slugging percentage, which equated to a 108 WRC+. Surprisingly, most of that success came from Jarren Duran, who hit leadoff 31 of the 101 games and had a 141 WRC+.
Roman Anthony hasn't performed in the first inning, but he has the rest of the game
Anthony has struggled in the leadoff spot all season. In a total of 36 games, the lefty has a .299 OPS in the first inning. In the second inning or later this season, Anthony boasts a .280/.395/.439/.834 slash line and a 136 WRC+. In those same innings, in only the games he was first in the batting order, he has a .792 OPS and 125 WRC+.
Something about him batting first in the first inning isn't working for him. Whether it's his approach or the way pitchers are attacking him in that spot, Anthony hasn't been able to put it together this season. That's why it's time to drop him down in the order.
That doesn't mean to all of a sudden move him down to seventh in the order, but to push him down to second or third and put a player with high on-base skills in front of him. The Sox have had a few players show really great on-base skills this season. Nick Sogard, Mickey Gasper, and Isiah Kiner-Falefa are all players with an OBP over .340 this season. Having one of them leadoff, then getting on base in front of Anthony, Ceddanne Rafaela, Willson Contreras, and Wilyer Abreu would be extremely dangerous.
Anthony hasn't shown he can hack it leading off the game this season; it's been his one real weak point since his return. With two weeks until the start of the playoffs and a postseason berth almost assured (100% per FanGraphs as of September 15th), now is the time to experiment with the lineup and fix this problem before they get to October.

Back in April, the Boston Red Sox's season was going off the rails.
The Red Sox started the season off with a 10-17 record and opted to fire a World Series-winning manager in Alex Cora — plus a handful of other coaches — and take a gamble by turning the reins over to interim manager Chad Tracy. At the time, it seemed like the sky was falling. That's because the losses kept piling up, so much so that the Red Sox were 14 games below .500 at 32-46 on June 25.
At the time, the season looked like a disaster. The Red Sox were trending towards being sellers ahead of the trade deadline, both Roman Anthony and Garrett Crochet were on the Injured List with no end in sight, and it seemed like chief baseball officer Craig Breslow's seat was getting hotter and hotter. But the Red Sox transformed their season and now, with the season winding down, ESPN's Buster Olney reported on Wednesday that the expectation is that both Breslow and Tracy will stay on with Boston beyond the 2026 season.
"But Breslow's vision of a team succeeding with pitching and defense fully manifested, and the Red Sox are closing in on a playoff berth and will likely face the Yankees in the wild-card round, again," Olney wrote. "Manager Chad Tracy has been working under an interim tag all season, something of a head-scratcher; it may be that the two sides talked about the idea of an extension in midseason but set aside the topic for the offseason. But Boston is now expected to retain both Breslow and Tracy."
The Red Sox Are Making The Right Call
This is undoubtedly the right call for the Red Sox at this time.
Let's start with Breslow. Whether you love him or not, he has built a team that can go on a run. Sure, there have been some misses over the last few years. Losing Alex Bregman was a public relations disaster. Not landing one of the big free agent bats, including Kyle Schwarber and Pete Alonso, this past offseason also was a surprise. But there are far more wins under Breslow's belt, than losses.
Sonny Gray is going to get Cy Young Award votes and has been Boston's ace this season. Ranger Suárez was an All-Star. Willson Contreras was an All-Star. Caleb Durbin is the heart and the soul of the 2026 Red Sox. Now, the Red Sox have an All-Star catcher on their hands in Adley Rutschman. Bringing back Mickey Gasper has turned into a game-changing move. And the list goes on. The Red Sox have a roster that can make noise.
On the Tracy front, there was obviously a learning curve to being a big league manager taking over during a season, especially in such a high-profile market, like Boston. He has handled the role with grace and has clearly gotten better as the year has gone on. Plus, it doesn't hurt that the Red Sox went on a historic 15-game winning streak and put together one of the best mid-season turnarounds in MLB history. All in all, these two should both be back in 2026 and it sounds like that will be the reality.

Ranger Suarez tossed his second straight seven-inning start and the Boston Red Sox scored in their final three at-bats en route to a 5-1 win over the visiting Kansas City Royals on Saturday afternoon.
Suarez (7-4) struck out eight, scattered five hits and allowed one run while completing his seven frames in 96 pitches as Boston (81-68) snapped its three-game losing streak.
Roman Anthony, Adley Rutschman and Nick Sogard each had multiple hits while Wilyer Abreu hit a two-run double that gave the Red Sox a sixth-inning lead they would not relinquish.
Carter Jensen’s 24th home run of the season marked the only scoring for Kansas City (66-83), which opened the series with a win Friday.
The Red Sox took the lead with two runs on three straight hits in the sixth. After Mickey Gasper and Rutschman knocked back-to-back singles to right to chase Royals starter Randy Dobnak (3-4), Abreu drove them home with a two-out double to deep center off reliever Anthony Gose.
The lead grew in each of the next two frames, beginning with Sogard hitting a leadoff double and scoring on Caleb Durbin’s RBI single off the Green Monster in the seventh.
After Garrett Whitlock struck out the side in the Royals’ eighth, Trevor Story and Sogard posted back-to-back doubles to plate another run.
Aroldis Chapman followed with a scoreless ninth to tab Suarez with the victory.
The teams plowed through three scoreless innings with just one baserunner: Bobby Witt Jr.’s one-out single in Kansas City’s opening frame. Suarez stranded him on third after recording back-to-back outs, including an inning-ending strikeout of Vinnie Pasquantino.
Suarez retired the Royals 1-2-3 on 10 pitches in the second and third innings while Dobnak faced the minimum, striking out three batters through the first third of the game.
In the fourth, Anthony turned a leadoff single through the right side into the opening run. After moving to second on Gasper’s grounder, Anthony scored when Rutschman knocked a single into center.
After finishing the fourth around Pasquantino’s two-out double, Suarez retired five straight before Jensen’s one-out solo homer inside Pesky’s Pole in the sixth. The southpaw stranded runners in the next two frames, including back-to-back strikeouts to cap the seventh.
–Field Level Media

Good morning! Last night, Chad Tracy gave at-bats to two pinch-hitters in the 8th inning: lefty killer Jahmai Jones and utility infielder Andruw Monasterio. Jones did his job in the 8th, singling to start the inning in place of Mickey Gasper, but would subsequently strike out to end the game in the 9th. Jones was a platoon revelation when he first arrived in Boston, but he's cooled off since then (a .200 batting average over his last 12 games), and his positional inflexibility makes him a difficult roster fit. Monasterio did not do his job last night. He struck out with the bases loaded, putting an end to the biggest threat the Sox had all night.
In light of last night's events it's time to ask: Is it time for Romy Gonzalez to get another crack? Romy theoretically combines the best of both Jones and Monasterio — he's a lefty-killer and a utility infielder. He struggled mightily in his (rushed) return to the Sox earlier this year and has recently been battling a nagging injury lately, but his AAA line reads .344/.400/.505 with 3 homers and 6 doubles. He could inject some pop just as the Sox look like they could use a little extra juice.

Romy Gonzalez seemed like a staple of the Boston Red Sox's offensive attack plan just a year ago. Now, with the playoffs looming, it's become difficult to see where he fits into the picture.
Having been demoted to Triple-A on Aug. 4, Gonzalez has been patiently waiting his turn. The Red Sox are used to having at least one right-handed bat on the roster who primarily gets his looks against left-handed pitchers, but Jahmai Jones has usurped that role from Gonzalez at least temporarily.
With 14 position players on the current active roster and likely 14 joining the Red Sox for the American League Wild Card Series in two weeks, there's an interesting conversation to have about Gonzalez now that the 30-year-old is having a hot month of September in Triple-A. Where will that conversation lead?
Is Gonzalez a legitimate threat to crack playoff roster?
Gonzalez batted near the top of the order for the Red Sox down the stretch last year whenever there was a lefty on the mound. But he also turned out to be battling a shoulder injury that necessitated surgery at the beginning of spring training and delayed his return to the majors until the end of June.
When he did make his season debut, Gonzalez recently admitted that he rushed his rehab, which might reasonably have thrown his swing out of whack against major league quality pitching. He went 12-for-65 with only one home run and a .572 OPS in his 19 major league games before his demotion.
“Where the team was at and all the injuries we had, it was my plan to kind of rush back and be up there,” Gonzalez said, via Christopher Smith of MassLive. “Obviously, hindsight’s 20/20.”
Now, with the Triple-A season coming to an end this weekend, Gonzalez has to know he might not make it back to the majors at all. But he's got the right attitude about the entire situation, seemingly.
“I’m ready whenever my name’s called,” Gonzalez said, per Smith.
If the Red Sox were going to put Gonzalez on the playoff roster, he'd likely have to displace either Connor Wong or Mickey Gasper. Nate Eaton, the current odd man out, should be replaced by Ceddanne Rafaela by the end of the week.

ARLINGTON, Texas — For the Red Sox, the vision of contention in 2026 seemed straightforward.
The team’s championship window had been pried open by the presence of a pair of cornerstones, with Garrett Crochet anchoring the rotation and Roman Anthony representing a lineup anchor not only for this year but several seasons to come.
But while the Sox are amid a magic-number countdown to a playoff berth, they’ve done so without Anthony and Crochet for most of the year. Their season has been saved in no small part by players who have emerged from obscurity to play critical roles — with essential contributions coming from Andruw Monasterio, Anthony Seigler, Mickey Gasper, Tsung-Che Cheng, Jahmai Jones, Tyron Guerrero, and more.
“I don’t think anybody had that on the drawing board,” said interim manager Chad Tracy with a chuckle. “They were asked to play a lot, and they produced. And if they didn’t, we were in trouble. It’s a huge piece of the 2026 season, no question.”
Of course, while no one expected the outsized impact of players who began the year as big league backups or in Triple-A, the Sox also took considerable pains to build organizational depth through a variety of transactions.
Whether it was an expanded version of the trade that brought Caleb Durbin from Milwaukee to include Monasterio and Seigler, or waiver claims of Cheng and Gasper, or a minor league deal for Guerrero, the season has been a case study in the notion that perceived little moves can have a huge impact.
“Every move and every decision matters,” said assistant general manager Mike Groopman, who oversees the team’s acquisitions group. “The big ones, whether it’s a larger free agent deal, [or] a larger, more high-profile trade, is naturally going to get a lot of attention.
“I don’t think this is unique to the Red Sox. There are 29 other teams that try to and do a very good job about caring about the ‘little’ things. But I think what we really try to reinforce is … that year over year, around the game, you see things that seem ‘little’ that end up being really impactful and big. [Deals that] seemed like small moves at the outset end up having a much, much larger impact commensurate with what would have been perceived at the time as a ‘larger’ move.”
Players who evolve from theoretical depth to become big league contributors excite numerous corners of an organization. The primary credit for those contributions, of course, belongs with a player, but they still often represent the combined efforts of personnel in scouting who identify the player’s potential contributions, player development personnel who help the player build on preexisting strengths and abilities in the minors, and big league staffers who help the players to perform at the game’s highest level.
Take Guerrero. After brief stints in the big leagues in 2018 and 2019, he’d become a journeyman, shuffling between organizations — and countries — but unable to forge a way back to the big leagues despite elite velocity.
But the Sox — who’d been interested in signing Guerrero before he pitched in the NPB in Japan in 2025 — remained intrigued, thanks in part to strong scouting recommendations from Kento Matsumoto in Japan and Manny Nanita in the Dominican Winter League. After they signed Guerrero to a minor league deal in the offseason, player development officials worked with him on some minor grip changes that unlocked significantly improved command with a sinker that regularly reached triple digits.
Guerrero’s dominance this year in Triple-A (0.92 ERA) essentially forced the Sox to call him up, and the 35-year-old emerged as a late-innings force from late June to late August (before shoulder fatigue led to a bad outing followed by a trip to the injured list), posting a 2.13 ERA over a 23-appearance stretch.
Again, the lion’s share of the credit goes to Guerrero for the work he did to fight his way back to the big leagues. But his emergence embodies the sort of under-the-radar acquisition that helped save the Sox’ season.
“The connection and integration between acquisition and development is really important,” said Groopman. “Guerrero and our [player development] group put a lot of time into [those changes] in the spring and the early season, to get him to a point where he was able to lock in some of these changes and unlock what was super obvious arm talent into something that was translating more consistently onto the major league mound.”
Of course, talent alone doesn’t dictate success once a depth player gets to the big leagues. They must also have the opportunity to contribute — and, in many cases, the freedom to fail while getting their bearings.
Tracy, who spent time with nearly all of this year’s depth contributors in Triple-A at the beginning of the year, has been mindful of creating an environment in which call-ups can contribute.
“I’m in the same boat [as them]. I want the freedom to go manage the game [as a first-time big league manager],” said Tracy. “I need to manage a game and feel like if I do something that doesn’t go right, it’s not the end of the world. If I feel that way, then I want the player to feel like, ‘Hey, if you go out there and play second base today and you make an error, move on to the next play.’
“If the culture becomes, ‘If I make a mistake, then all of a sudden I clam up and I get really tight,’ we’re going to have a problem. So you look at them and say, ‘You’re here for a reason: To go play your game. Don’t worry about making a mistake. Move on to the next pitch, next play.’ And they did that, and they were awesome.”

item.content:encoded:
Patrick Sandoval has had a rocky month. Entering Tuesday, the Red Sox left-hander had allowed a 6.12 ERA over his last five starts, but coming out of the gate Sandoval looked like he’d finally figured things out.
But after striking out the first four batters he faced, the wheels came off in the bottom of the second.
Sandoval allowed four runs over an interminable 44-pitch second inning and ultimately got the hook after recording just eight outs in Boston’s 4-2 loss to the Texas Rangers.
Nick Sogard hit a two-run home run to help get the Red Sox back into the game, but the offense otherwise couldn’t get anything going against Jacob deGrom and the Rangers bullpen, squandering bases loaded opportunities in the fifth and eighth innings.
Sandoval started strong by striking out the side in the first inning, but after sending down Jake Burger to start the second everything ground to a screeching halt. The right-hander allowed a pair of singles, served up a two-run double to Elias Diaz, and then walked back-to-back batters to load the bases for five-time All-Star Corey Seager.
It appeared for a moment like Sandoval might minimize the damage when he drew a pop fly to shallow left, but the ball drifted into no-man’s land and Trevor Story couldn’t make the catch, allowing two more runs to score and putting the Rangers up 4-0.
Sandoval ultimately needed 44 pitches to get through the second, blowing up his pitch count and ensuring a long evening for the Red Sox bullpen. He recorded two outs in the third and was lifted for Brayan Bello after allowing four runs over 2 2/3 innings.
“They drug at bats out on him,” Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy told reporters in Arlington postgame. “It looked like he was going to get out of there with Diaz, that was a long at bat, I think one of those pitches was close and then he hits the double in the corner and it was just a struggle, we just couldn’t get out of the inning.”
Four runs matches the largest deficit the Red Sox have overcome in a win this season, but the club didn’t need long to cut it in half. After Caleb Durbin reached on a one-out single in the top of the third, Sogard ripped a line drive off deGrom that cleared the right field fence for a two-run home run.
It was the fifth home run of the season for Sogard, all of which have come since Aug. 19. Prior to that the 29-year-old had never hit a homer over his first three seasons as a big leaguer.
That wound up being as close as Boston got.
The Red Sox could have tied the score or taken the lead with one swing in the fifth inning, but despite loading the bases without recording a hit the club couldn’t get a run across. Jarren Duran was hit by a pitch, Durbin reached on catcher’s interference and Mickey Gasper walked to bring up Adley Rutschman with two outs, but the catcher grounded out to short to keep it a 4-2 game.
Boston’s bullpen did its part to keep the Red Sox in the game. Bello tossed 1 2/3 perfect innings, Alec Gamboa threw one scoreless aided in large part by a brilliant double play turned by Sogard to end the fifth, and Wyatt Olds worked his way out of a runners-at-the-corners, two-out jam to escape the sixth. Jovani Moran entered with a man on in the seventh and got three quick outs, setting the table for one last Red Sox push in the eighth.
Jahmai Jones sparked the rally with a leadoff single, Willson Contreras drew a one-out walk, and after Wilyer Abreu grounded out to move the two runners into scoring position Story was intentionally walked to load the bases again.
Rather than have Duran face the left-hander Jacob Latz, Tracy pinch hit Andruw Monasterio, but the move didn’t pay off. Monasterio worked a full count and nearly went deep on a hard hit liner that landed just foul before striking out to leave them loaded again.
Boston went quietly in the top of the ninth, finishing the game 0 for 4 with runners in scoring position while stranding nine men on base.
“We gave ourselves a couple of opportunities to maybe hit a single and tie the game up and we couldn’t do it tonight,” Tracy said.
Magic number still 5
In addition to keeping pace in the AL West race, the Rangers also jumped the Toronto Blue Jays to become the first team below the AL Wild Card cutline. As a result the Red Sox’s magic number remains five despite the Blue Jays’ 10-1 loss earlier in the night.
Boston (82-69) can clinch a playoff berth as early as Friday, and depending on how things play out in the AL Central the Red Sox could lock down the second Wild Card spot as soon as this weekend.
Houck scoreless with WooSox
Tanner Houck (Tommy John surgery rehab) tossed a scoreless inning of relief in his latest rehab appearance with the WooSox on Tuesday. The right-hander entered the game in the seventh inning and allowed one walk, no hits and struck out three over 22 pitches.
